beta_new: Two start variations exist: the original 1951 Route, which is faster but includes a 'scary' 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds roughly 500 ft of climbing on more logical terrain to avoid it. On the 1957 line, initial 4th-class terrain leads into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby ~60-ft horizontal gully traverse (5.5) with minimal protection, and steep heather sections requiring careful, finger-pressing technique. On the right-hand (1957) rib, a roughly 700-ft crux section of higher-quality 5.6 rock climbing leads toward a bivy site beside the glacier, below the snow arete and glacier that lead to the summit.

Start on the Bad-Tempered Prom Queen pitch (5.8+/FA: John Goodrum) located on a low-angle bulge just left of vine maple, serving as the approach to the upper pitches. Longer pitches include approximately 10-11 clips. Pitches 1 and 6 are notably stiff 5.8s. Fixed lines assist with the traverse between pitches 4-5. Plan for 6+ hours total for ascent and descent. The route is hot in summer—climb early in the day. Communication between climber and belayer may be difficult on upper pitches in wind.
Two parallel bolts partway up allow going right or left around mini-roofs — left is the recommended line. About 20 ft of sustained climbing; most of the rest is easier.
Small holds lead through a little bulge to easier 5.2 ground and the chain anchor.

From the Denny Creek Trailhead, hike the Denny Creek Trail past Keekwulee and Snowshoe Falls to Melakwa Lake, cross talus toward Melakwa Pass (the saddle between Kaleetan and Chair Peak), then follow the scramble trail up the crest of Kaleetan's south ridge to the summit block. The route is mostly a well-worn boot path with a stretch of Class 2-3 scrambling and one short rock-chimney crux near 5,100 ft.

A solid, short alpine rock route consisting of three pitches on granite with excellent anchor systems. The route is mostly low 5th class climbing with sound rock quality throughout most of the climb, though the first pitch contains some loose material. Multiple fixed anchors and bolts make the route straightforward and relatively safe for well-executed rock climbing skills. The climb features excellent views of Liberty Bell and the surrounding North Cascades.

From a high camp in Mesahchie Basin (~6,600 ft), climbers ascend northwest to gain the Katsuk-Mesahchie col area, then work up scree/talus and short rock steps to a bench around 7,400 ft (the last ~100 ft is Class 4). Above the bench, several ribs and gullies lead up through mixed scree, heather, and solid rock; the standard finish follows a leftward-trending gully whose lower half is hidden behind a buttress and which tops out just below the summit's "mushroom" block. In early season (before roughly August) this gully can hold continuous steep snow exceeding 45°, requiring an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing experience; a small moat often opens along the left edge of the snowfield late season. The summit block itself is climbed via a series of blocks on its west side, Class 3. No technical rock climbing or roped pitches are required by late summer, but the terrain is sustained, loose, and route-finding is nontrivial.

The standard line follows the maintained PCT north from the Snoqualmie Pass trailhead for roughly 4.6-5 miles (up to 5.5 mi one-way depending on exact trailhead/summit points used), then breaks off onto a faint, unsigned boot path near 5,200 ft that climbs directly uphill to the ridge and summit. No technical gear is required in summer conditions; it is popular as a long day hike/scramble combo with the nearby Kendall Katwalk viewpoint.

From a high camp in the basin below Mesahchie Peak, climbers side-hill traverse west along Kimtah's south face at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft, crossing more than a dozen loose ribs and gullies (mostly class 3). A well-known 'red ledge' cuts across the ribs and greatly simplifies the route-finding. Near the 'Grotesque Gendarmes,' the standard line downclimbs about 150 ft down a buttress and threads a narrow, exposed class 4 gully to bypass a cliff band, then regains the traverse. A final broad, solid-granite gully (class 3) leads up to the ridge just west of the true summit, finishing with a short class 3 scramble across a scree saddle between the west and east (true, 8,649 ft) summits.

Grade: IV 5.11+ alpine rock climb (5.12a on some topos). Route length: 900 feet (8 pitches) on West Face Wall. First free ascent: September 9, 2016, by Sol Wertkin with Jon Gleason. Route climbs first 4 pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, moves left onto Gorillas Direct (2 pitches), then climbs 2-pitch direct finish up aesthetic splitter crack on overhanging headwall (5.11d-5.12a crux). Connector pitch (5.10b): roof bulge, stem-box, runout overhanging jug climbing. Headwall pitch (5.11d-5.12a): slabby steps, vertical features, meaty hand/fist jams, wild layback sequences. Required gear: double rack cams/nuts (small-medium), two fixed nuts at headwall top. Best season: late summer through early September (before fall storms and snow). Hazards: significant runouts between protection placements, loose rock with hidden chock stones, 30+ meters of overhanging exposure on headwall, alpine weather exposure risk (unplanned bivy possible).

From the 7,900-ft Klawatti-Austera Col (an easy side-trip from Klawatti Col), gain the lower part of the north ridge — easiest on its east side — and scramble Class 3 terrain to a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' (roughly 8,400 ft). Circumnavigate the Smokestack on its west side via a short gully to regain the ridge crest, then follow the crest to the summit. About 1 hour from the Klawatti-Austera Col, up to 2 hours from the main Klawatti Col.

Grade III alpine route requiring mixed climbing technique. Approach via Klawatti Glacier from the west with one short Class 4-5 rock step over the bergschrund followed by several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow. Crampons, ice axe, pickets, 60m rope, and single rack to 2 inch are essential. Allow 1-2 hours for climbing depending on amount of roped climbing.

Climbers finishing the summit scramble use this short pitch to reach the fixed rappel anchors. Start on the slab to the right of the crack, traverse onto it, then climb the wide, left-trending crack to a small sandy flat, and traverse left toward a cairn marking the bolted rap station.

Kololo Peaks presents three viable multi-day approaches, all exceeding 12 miles and typically requiring 2-3 days with glacier travel. The climb itself is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on talus and snow, with the primary challenge being glacier crevasse navigation and length of approach rather than technical difficulty. Neither summit presents hard climbing; the route involves walking across easy terrain between the west summit and the slightly higher east summit (8,240 ft, the true high point).

moves.from: The standard route from the west via North Fork Sauk Trail offers the most established access, climbing through old-growth forest to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, then traversing multiple glacier systems.

beta_new: An enjoyable alpine route, and the most direct of the three approaches to Kyes. From the northeast base of the peak (~6,000 ft), Class 3 rock along the climber's-left edge of the Pride Glacier leads to the summit via its southeast corner. Glacier travel (crevasses reported) and route-finding through Quartz Basin's cliff bands on the approach add seriousness beyond the rock grade alone.

From a camp at La Bohn Lakes or La Bohn Gap, climbers head west from the gap up boulders and heather onto the east ridge. Parties describe crossing to a false summit just short of the true top, with roughly the final 1/8 mile being a walk along the summit ridge. The line is entirely off-trail Class 2-3 talus with no technical climbing required in summer conditions.

This alpine ice/snow route ascends a north-facing couloir just left (climber's) of the Zipper, with two or three steeper sections requiring ice protection along the way, topping out on a ridge above the Zipper route. From the top, climbers typically rappel 100+ ft (double rope recommended) into the adjacent Zipper couloir, then climb the last of the Zipper and traverse to the summit.

The route's crux is packed into the first ten feet: a technical, pumpy opening sequence that has caused many climbers to fall low. Once past this tricky start, the remaining climbing to the anchor is comparatively reasonable. Photos of the line show technical hooking/mixed-tool sequences, indicating it is regularly dry-tooled as well as rock-climbed.

From a base camp between the two Yang Yang Lakes, the route heads south around a forested ridge and ascends talus to a distinctive 'secret stair' — a precipitous path up compacted dirt and rock through a small gully to a grassy ledge. From there it follows the ridgeline to a rock outcropping beneath Le Conte's North Face, then works around (avoiding) Peak 7004 via east-slope talus and snow before an exposed traverse of narrow, loose ledges gains the summit. Rated class 4 scrambling; a rope, ice axe, and crampons are standard given the glacier travel required just to reach the peak.

P1: fun chimney far right on the wall past a small tree, onto a knobby slab with thin corner pro, a spicy 5.8 move left onto another slab, into a corner belay (~30m). P2: fun corner to a flake, move left around it (5.9) into a corner with knobby feet to a large ledge (~30m). P3: left-facing wide lieback corner (#4 Camalot helpful), leave the corner left via delicate face moves to a rampy hand crack, then shorter blocky corners to a large ledge below the roof pitch (~60m). P4: white knobby rock to a small roof with small gear, over the roof and up crack/knobs to a ledge belay (~45m). P5: 4th-class terrain moving up-left toward the summit, steepening to low-5th class near the top — simul-climbing works well; roughly 100m to the summit block.

Day 1 follows the well-graded Lena Lake Trail 3 miles to Lena Lake, then a steep, primitive trail up West Fork Lena Creek to Upper Lena Lake (6.5 mi, 4,000 ft gain from the trailhead). Day 2 leaves the trail entirely: climb southwest across meadows/heather toward the ridge south of Mt Lena, follow intermittent way trails west past Scout Lake, over Scout Pass (5,200 ft) and Upper Scout Lake/Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass (5,000 ft, with views of the 'Ullin's Bathtubs' tarns), then up the steep snow/dirt 'St. Peter's Ramp' to St. Peter's Gate (5,950 ft) — the high point of the traverse and an obvious notch in Mt Stone's SE ridge. Lake of the Angels lies half a mile southwest of the gate in a grassy bowl. The optional Mt Stone summit side-trip climbs a class 3-4 gully on the mountain's south face to a rock bowl, joins the standard west-ridge route, and finishes with a class 2-3 scramble on solid pillow basalt to the summit (about 1,100 ft gain round trip, ~3 hrs). Day 3 descends the Putvin Trail — historic and primitive, with cliff sections (one with a fixed handline, one requiring tree roots) past Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet — to the Putvin Trailhead, about 4 miles by road from the Lena Lake Trailhead where the trip began.

P1-P2 (5.7, then 5.10c): start as for the West Face up broken ledges, then take the thin-hands splitter on the left. P3 (5.12a, crux): strenuous climbing moves left past 2 bolts, then a splitter to a 2-bolt belay. P4 (5.11a): carry on up the crack system. P5 (5.11c/5.11+): hard, steep moves up the obvious dihedral. P6 (5.11c/5.11+): grab the thin jug flake, move left into a crack and finish with bouldery moves. P7 (5.10a): wander right, then traverse a slab back left. P8-P9 (5.9, 5.8): knobs around the left edge of a roof, then blocky cracks on the crest to the summit ridge.

Start on low-angle dihedral left of Lexington-Minuteman gully. Ascend via cracks and chimneys; crux is pitch 5 with exposed traverse. Upper pitches are off-width and chimney climbing. Standard trad rack essential; doubles to #3 plus a #4, with a single #5 or #6 useful for the short wide sections.

moves.from: Exit via notch, descend west gully.

rows.sizes: single #5 or #6 for the short wide sections

value.text: Cams in doubles to #3, a #4, and a single #5 or #6 for the short wide sections.

moves.from: doubles to #3 plus a #4, with a single #5 or #6 useful for the short wide sections

beta_new: About 200 m of climbing with two short 5.12- cruxes on solid edges and thin cracks; two pitches overlap the line of the older aid route Liberty Loop. Cruxes are mostly short boulder problems that lead to good holds, though protection sometimes requires committing above your last piece.

P1 (5.10b/c) climbs a face-and-crack system to bolts on a slab, needing 4-5 gear placements before the first bolt. P2 (5.11c) steps left off the anchor, following rightward-trending bolts with room for a finger-sized piece. P3 (5.12a) follows bolts up and left through sustained, hard-to-aid climbing (bring a .5, .75 and #1 Camalot). P4 (5.11c) starts with an awkward, rough 5.10c traverse left into Liberty Crack; the section above to the anchor is 5.11+ R, though it can feel closer to PG13.

Pitches range from 5.6 to 5.11b, with the crux at P3a (5.10d) described as balancey, technical climbing on mediocre gear. Notable features include an offwidth section, sustained hand cracks, Medusa's Roof on P12, and a class-4 scramble finishing the route. No bolted belay stances exist except where the route intersects Liberty Crack.

First climbed wall-style in 1966 by Bertulis and McPherson, freed in 1991 by Steve Risse and Keith Hertel without adding fixed gear (partly yo-yo style over 2 days), and given its first ground-up redpoint in 2009 by Jens Holsten and Max Hasson. Sustained 5.10-5.12 climbing through named features like the Baer Ceiling, Cascade Ceilings, and Well Hung Ceiling.

From the Liberty-Concord notch, either a runout 5.8R left variation (poor pro for ~30 ft) or the original line up the top of the notch ramp reach a shared anchor; pitch 2 climbs up and right to a clean white dihedral to a sloping ledge with chain anchors.

Grade III alpine rock, 5.11 crux. Four pitches on Liberty Bell West Face. Pitch 1 (5.8): Slab moves left into corner with short bulge. Pitch 2 (5.11 crux): Steep, awkward fist crack past the right side of a roof, physical, excellent gear. Pitch 3 (5.10): Left-angling hand crack with roof/bulge exit. Pitch 4 (5.7): Navigate tunnel or harder left slab variation, then simul/scramble on exposed sunny arete to summit. Excellent hand crack climbing with minimal traffic. Hazards: loose rock from freeze-thaw cycles, afternoon thunderstorms, exposure on final arete.

moves.from: Approach via Beckey Route approach, staying left at fork in gully.

beta_new: Grade: 5.12 (YDS), Grade IV overall. 11 pitches, approximately 1,100 feet of climbing. Route follows intricate crack systems and faces on East Face of Liberty Bell. Hazards: significant rock fall danger in approach gully (parties above knock rock down it, bowling-alley style); loose rock throughout approach; exposed alpine terrain; weather exposure on big wall. Required skills: advanced alpine rock climbing, 5.11+ crack climbing, self-rescue, anchor building, multi-pitch experience. First ascent: 1967 (aid climbing); free ascent variation established 2008 by Mikey Schaefer. Best season: June-September; July-September strongly preferred (late June requires ice axe, crampons). Notable: route features substantial fixed gear on most pitches.

moves.from: ; descent via two-rope rappel from M&M Ledge or summit traverse

beta_new: Follows Liberty Crack's original aid line but climbed entirely free; pitch 1 (5.11-) leads to the crux pitch 2 'Lithuanian Lip' (5.13b) - a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip and committing moves to a small stance. A slab variation on pitch 3 (5.12) avoids the original bolt ladder.

Grade V alpine, 5.9 YDS, 26 pitches, approximately 2,000 ft (606 m) of climbing. Route composition: Beckey Route on Liberty Bell (5.3-5.6), North Face of Concord Tower, North Face of Lexington Tower, Northwest Corner of North Early Winter Spire (5.9+), Southwest Rib of South Early Winter Spire. Hazards include significant rockfall danger in the approach gully, which funnels falling rock like a bowling alley, exposed alpine terrain, route finding challenges. Requires excellent trad climbing skills, solid alpine rock climbing experience, and good protection/anchor placement ability. Standard rack with couple bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire. Short rappel descent from summits. The individual summits, the Beckey Route above all, are busy on summer weekends, though few parties do the full traverse. Best season: July-August during optimal weather windows. Typically done as 1-2 day alpine climb with experienced parties.

rows.sizes: a couple of bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire

value.text: A standard rack with a couple of bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire.

moves.from: Standard rack with couple bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire.

beta_new: Standard summer/fall line to the summit: trail to Lake Valhalla, then off-trail travel up southeast-facing slopes to a saddle on the southeast ridge and along the ridge to the top. No rope or technical rock gear is needed in dry conditions; the same slopes are also skinned/skied or snowshoed as a separate winter tour when snow-covered.

The ridge is an obvious ski-touring objective in winter. In summer it is a 7-mile, 2,100-foot scramble starting from the first switchback on Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and following the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail to a saddle on the southeast ridge. Jim Brisbine's party climbed it as a rock scramble over 20-21 September 1975, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and continuing over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn before descending the west ridge. The winter version has you leave the road at the first major hairpin, head southwest up wooded and steep but always snowshoeable hillside, traverse toward Lichtenwasser Lake at about 4,600 ft (crossing the lake if it is frozen), then take easy slopes to the ridge crest and follow the summit ridge to the top. A winter north-side version is given with compass bearings: ski 2.6 miles up Smithbrook Road, leave it before the major switchback near 3,970 ft, follow a true bearing of 177 degrees to Lichtenwasser Lake, then 248 degrees from the lake's south end to a 5,640-foot saddle, and ascend the southeast ridge to the summit — about 5.2-plus miles, rated 2 to 2+ in skill and 2-minus in fitness, and included among the classic backcountry ski and snowboard routes in Washington. Avalanche hazard is the defining concern; both sides of the mountain present it.

James Nakagami climbed the West Face at 5.9+ with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall. A grand west face is one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and one party was turned around by the sheer wall before reaching the summit by an easier line, which confirms that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.

Historic climbing-club parties describe an off-trail approach from the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus trailhead via Union Gap and Lichtenberg Pass, then a rock climb up the west face and west rib of the west peak, with descent down the easier northeast slope back toward the start. Little is known about grade and protection; treat this as an obscure, lightly-traveled line rather than a well-established route.

Start on the northwest face just right of the prominent hanging glacier with a 60 m WI4 pitch, the route's crux, shared with Shooting Gallery on neighbouring Assassin Spire; its upper half is overhanging, poorly protected ice of doubtful quality. Above, cross a snowfield and climb a vertical ice curtain and a well-protected step of glacial ice into the upper amphitheater, the basin between Lincoln Peak and Assassin Spire, simul-climbing along its west side. On Lincoln's northwest wall, about four roped pitches of steeper ice follow, with snowfields up to 70° between them; the obvious central flow gives about 120 m of WI3+ in two long pitches. From the upper snowfield, follow a rime-covered ridge to a sub-summit, downclimb a short rime step, and climb a final icy gully to the summit.

The historic standard route on Lincoln Peak; the only other line is a rarely formed northwest-face ice route. Technical snow and ice climbing with significant avalanche risk. Route comprises multiple sections: 30-40 degree initial snowfields, crux serac obstacle requiring 70-85 degree ice climbing (50 feet high), hidden gully with 2-4 foot deep runnels, narrow exposed snow aretes with steep drop-offs, and final 50-degree gully to summit rocks. Climb early morning when snow is frozen; conditions deteriorate rapidly with afternoon warming.

moves.from: Approach via Rankin Creek Basin from FS Road 38.

beta_new: The route climbs the gully/face system above a col south of the peak. Parties approach via Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek to a tarn/col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft, then scramble ~100 ft of easy Class 3 talus before roping up for two full 60m pitches of low-5th-class granite (a crack/slab pitch, then a rightward traverse into a chimney), finishing with a short Class 3 section through boulders to the summit plateau. One notable hazard is a ~20-ft unprotectable 5.6 slab section below the approach col with no crack systems for gear.

From the pass, head roughly south-southwest past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes toward Little Annapurna's northeast ridge, then follow cairns up open granite slabs and talus on the peak's north side to the summit -- one of three rocky high points on the ridge, with the true summit being the middle one. The line itself involves minimal exposure and only occasional Class 3 moves, but Aasgard Pass is the physical and route-finding crux of the day.

moves.from: From the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trailhead, hike to Colchuck Lake and grind up the steep boulder-and-scree gully of Aasgard Pass to reach the upper Enchantment basin.
